text: We now have every piece needed to read an image: convolutions to detect local patterns, activations to bend, pooling to summarise, and fully connected layers to make a decision. Let us assemble a complete convolutional network for a familiar task, recognising handwritten digits in small greyscale images twenty-eight pixels on a side, and follow the shape of the data all the way through.

The image enters as a single channel. The first convolution applies eight kernels of size three by three, with a border of padding so that the size is kept, producing eight feature maps of twenty-eight by twenty-eight, and a ReLU bends every value. Max pooling then halves each map to fourteen by fourteen. The data has become a stack of eight smaller maps, each recording where its own pattern appears.

The second convolution is where channels meet. Each of its sixteen kernels is not a flat three by three square but a three by three by eight block, because it reads all eight maps from the layer below and combines them into one new map. After a ReLU and another pooling step we have sixteen maps of seven by seven. The picture has become smaller in space but richer in kinds of feature, trading information about where for information about what.

Now the spatial layout has served its purpose. We flatten the sixteen maps into one long vector of seven hundred and eighty-four numbers, and a fully connected layer maps it to ten scores, one for each digit. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities, cross-entropy compares them with the true label, and backpropagation sends gradients back through the dense layer, the pooling and the convolutions alike, so every kernel learns.

Counting parameters reveals something interesting. The first convolution has only eighty, the second just over a thousand, but the final dense layer has nearly eight thousand. Convolutions are cheap because their weights are shared across positions, and in classic networks most parameters sit in the fully connected layers at the end, which is one reason later designs replaced them with global average pooling.

This design goes back to Yann LeCun's LeNet, which read handwritten digits on bank cheques in the 1990s. In 2012 AlexNet, a much larger network of the same kind trained on graphics processors, won the ImageNet competition by a wide margin, and that result set off the deep learning boom that eventually led to today's language models.

A language model has the same overall skeleton. Its input is turned into vectors, passed through a stack of repeated blocks, and a final linear layer produces scores, now one for every token in the vocabulary, which softmax turns into probabilities. Next we meet the residual connection, the small trick that made very deep networks trainable.
